title: Human artifacts look simple because engineering requires predictability

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Human artifacts look simple because engineering requires predictability

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Human-made artifacts tend to look simpler than natural objects because engineers need to foresee what their systems will do, which requires computational reducibility, whereas nature has no such constraint and many natural systems are computationally irreducible.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: And I believe the basic answer to this has to do with the fact that when we as humans set up artifacts we usually need to be able to foresee what they will do—for otherwise we have no way to tell whether they will achieve the purposes we want.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Intelligence in the Universe” (from p. 822), p. 828. Scope: human engineering artifacts compared with natural objects

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-48: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.40

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing images can test a narrow descriptive proxy, but they do not measure computational reducibility or the engineering motive claimed as the cause. The full explanation is therefore only partly resolvable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Construct matched image and dynamical datasets of artifacts and natural objects, quantify structural and predictive complexity, and relate artifact complexity to documented design requirements. A robust reversed difference challenges the descriptive part, but causal attribution requires controlling function, materials, and selection.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Visual simplicity is metric-dependent.

Function, scale, material, and selection confound natural-artifact comparisons.

Image datasets do not contain engineering predictability requirements.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public shape and organism repositories can support a statistical comparison of how regular designed objects look relative to natural ones, which is the observable surface of the claim. They do not record whether a designer needed a predictive theory, and many non-computational constraints produce simple artifacts. The available comparison is a proxy with serious confounds.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare compressibility or geometric regularity of human-designed objects with natural objects in matched shape or image corpora. A robust simplicity gap is the surface prediction. The causal clause, that engineers must foresee behavior, needs a contrast with designed objects that were not required to be predictable.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Artifact and organism collections are unmatched samples.

A photograph does not measure whether a natural system is computationally irreducible.

Materials, style, and function produce simple forms without any appeal to computational reducibility.
